To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

The presence of tumour makers was relatively common in human bronchogenic carcinoma and there appeared to be no association between the presence or absence of any given tumour marker and the presence or absence or any other marker or the histological type of the lung tumour.
the presence of tumor markers is relatively common.

1) CEA, B1P, and hCG-beta were the most frequently detected antigens; 2) CEA was detected in the highest percentage of tumour cells; 3) CEA, hCG-beta, and B1P were the most frequently co-expressed antigens; and 4) there was no correlation between the expression of tumour markers and tumour type.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an immunological assay for the detection of human lung carcinoma.
the development of a new method for the detection of cancer in the lung.
the development of an in vitro assay to detect the presence of human chorionic-like gonadotropin (HCG) in human serum and urine.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of these tumour markers in lung carcinoma does not necessarily imply a primary pulmonary origin of the tumour.
the presence of these markers in lung tumours is of little value for the purpose of tumour classification.
the presence of any of the tumour markers studied is of no value in the histological diagnosis of lung cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the tumours studied were positive in varying proportions for six different antigens.
the presence of any tumour marker is not of prognostic value in lung carcinoma.

there was no correlation between the presence of one marker and another, and that the presence of any one of these six tumour markers was not associated with any particular histological type of tumour.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of a given tumour marker does not appear to be associated with the presence of any of the others, nor with histological type.
the presence of a marker in a tumour does not necessarily mean that the tumour will respond to treatment with the corresponding hormone.
the presence of a marker does not appear to be associated with any particular histological type of tumour, nor does the presence of one marker appear to predict the presence of any others.
